SHRI FALI S. NARIMAN (Nominated): Sir, during this debate on 
the Budget, the hon. Members have a ttacked the Government, the hon. 
Members have supported the Government, but I would appeal to all sections 
of this House to congratulate the Government, not for this Budget, but for 
nominating to this House such a fine, distinguished economist, Mr. Jalan, 
who just spoke. He has made a signal of non-political contribution and 
helped to raise the level of debate. 
Sir, I have been in this House for nearly four years, and the single 
fact that has most impressed me during this period is the consistent, low-key 
and soft soft approach of the Leader of the House only to be matched with the 
soft-voiced and eloquent response of the Leader of the Opposition. I have 
great admiration for each of them. Desp ite great provocation at times, I have 
never seen or heard them ever raising their 
101 

RAJYA SABHA [5 February, 2004] 
voices or ever raising the rhetoric of the debate. And I often wonder, and I 
tell my hon. colleagues why all of us cannot emulate these two leading 
figures in this House of Elders. 
The equable temperament of the Finance Minister, I believe, is 
reflected in his speech on the Interim Budget. There are no extravagant 
claims, no beating of the drum, except at least one of the concessions that are 
announced is apparently given with a view to impending elections. He that 
runs may read them. "The recommendation of the Fifth Central Pay 
Commission Report that DA should be merged with basic pay wherever DA 
exceeds 50 per cent of pay has been fasten ed on." to merge DA to the extent 
of 50 per cent of pay with effect from 1 st April, 2004 and is clearly a wooing 
of a large segment of voters, namely, the Government servants, without the 
financial implications of inflation of this very large benefit. I wish the 
Finance Minister had used the same rational, restrainted language, which he 
used in paragraph 31, when speaking about reviving upwards the standard 
deduction for income-tax purposes. He said: This question needs to be 
revisited."   I wish he had said that. 
But, Sir, having said all this, unlike my learned colleagues, I have no 
figures to offer; I have no figures to refute. I have only some apprehensions to 
voice. I have uppermost in my mind what the Finance Minister said in the 
opening paragraph of his speech. He ha s said, "Growth statistics are very 
important; they are vital inputs." But, for that reason, he says ( that it is 
important for us to have, what he calls, 'gross national contentment' for an era 
of distributive justice. 'It is-he says-- the catalyst that motivates redoubled 
national endeavour." I agree. I like this phrase 'gross national contentment' 
because, as a non-party Member, it enables me to ventilate my apprehensions. 
The country will see greater and greater  economic prosperity, and, if you 
pardon my saying so, without reference to whichever Government is there, 
because I always believe that the count ry is always greater than all the 
Governments it has had and it will ever have. The Finance Minister envisages 
in his Interim Budget Sp eech that there will be greater national contentment 
leading to national endeavour. But let us please examine what this means. It 
means greater contentment for all sections  of the society; not for one section, 
not for one community, not for one class, but for all. 
I have an apprehension when I see visions of economic prosperity. 
Like the Finance Minister but I also see visions of growing intolerance and 
religious bigotry and, sometimes, visions of hate, and, as a member of a 
102 

[5 February, 2004] RAJYA SABHA 
minority community, I sometimes shudder. I also see visions of more and 
more unemployment and more and more jobless; and we cannot have national 
contentment, unless the minorities, the j obless, the unemployed, particularly, 
the educated unemployed, are given hop e and avenues of progress. We are a 
pluralistic society with manifold cultures. We have a large pluralist populace. 
If your party, Mr. Finance Minister, envi sages victory in the elections, then I 
wish you godspeed. But I request your party to remember the words of 
wisdom of a great English Prime Minister. When the Nazis were knocking at 
the doors of England during the time of the World War, he too had visions of 
victory. He said-those words are now famous--"in war, determination; in 
peace, goodwill; in defeat, de fiance; but in victory,  magnanimity". If you are 
victorious in these elections, as you hope to be, you must, and I repeat you 
must, be magnanimous to all sections of the society. Victory must not breed a 
sense of arrogance. Only then will you be able to truly have what you 
envisage, a gross national contentment,  because after the party wins the 
elections, whatever the party, it must ca rry the country with it. Only then will 
there be national contentment. Victory is good; but integrity of the country, as 
a whole, is better. "Feel good" is a nice slogan. But I would respectfully 
suggest feel happy and feel secure" is a far better slogan. Thank you. 
SHRI P.O. ALEXANDER (Maharasht ra): Mr. Vice-Chairman, Sir, 
while listening to the various speeches in the Parliament and following the 
comments on the Interim Budget in th e media, I find that there are two 
streams of criticisms. One criticism is that the Interim Budget has been a 
give-away Budget, a populist Budget, a Budget which has been prepared with 
an eye on the elections and, theref ore, it had exceeded the conventional 
boundaries of an Interim Budget or Vote-on-Account. The second stream of 
criticism against the Interim Budget is that it has not given enough or it has 
not addressed some of the important concerns of the nation. It like 
employment generation and rural development. When you look at these two 
streams of criticisms, I feel that I should congratulate the Finance Minister for 
producing an Interim Budget where cr iticisms from both sides are cancelling 
each other. I feel that it has neither been a give-away Budget nor a closed-fist 
Budget; it has been a Budget relevant to the needs of the economy at this time 
and I would call it a very timely Budget. My esteemed friend, Shri Bimal 
Jalan, said that he was a great admirer of the Finance Minister and he had an 
opportunity of working with him. I never had an opportunity of working with 
him,  but having listened to the two Budgets

RAJYA SABHA [5 February, 2004]

robust political sense. In fact, if you take  the list of Finance Ministers of this

points which I hope he will take into account when he presents the major

Madam, I am very grateful to all the hon. Members who have benefited the 
Government with their views, observations, comments, criticism and advice. I 
am mindful, Madam, of the time as to how it is not even the schedules of 
today that are lengthening, but how the schedule of the dissolution of the 
other House is also now lengthening. The other House awaits our message 
about what we need to decide, and till such time as we do not send our 
message, they too cannot take their decisions. I will, therefore, be as brief as I 
can. But even in the process of being brief, I will endeavour to address as 
many of the issues as have been raised. It is possible that I might not be able 
to answer each and every sp ecific point because that, in such a debate, might 
not be possible. Broadly, Madam, my good friend from the Opposition, the 
initiator of the debate, particularly Pranabbabu and others from the 
Opposition have charged me with two things. One is that in the Interim 
Budget, I have made a political statement. This is rather a curious charge, 
Madam, because as my friend, Shri Ar un Shourie said, it is  like charging the 
political activitists by behaving like a politician. It is difficult for me, 
therefore, to otherwise rebut this ch arge. Every economic document, if it 
claims that it is innocent of politics, is not making a correct claim. 
The second broad observation from most of the hon. Members of the 
Opposition is that you are asserting that  there, is a feel-good factor; some 
have called it 'good feel factor'. But, wh atever way you call it, there is a feel 
good factor, but we are not feeling good. I take on board that the Opposition 
is not feeling good; the country is feeli ng good. They do not agree, but, then, 
it is an altogether different remedy that would be required, if they are not 
feeling good. Hon. Pranabbabu did me the singular honour,

FAREWELL TO RETIRING MEMBERS 
MR. CHAIRMAN: Hon. Members, today we bid farewell to some 
of our colleagues who are retiring at different points of time in the next three 
months after completion of their term of office. I am sure, some of the retiring 
members would get re-elected. We in the House will certainly miss those who 
are not returning. 
As a Presiding Officer, I shall certainly miss the passion of their 
arguments and the liveliness of their sp eeches. At times, I had to face their 
high temper and annoyance, but, I also  appreciate their sense of humour and 
courtesy that they had always shown towards me. 
The membership of Rajya Sabha is in itself a great honour, may, I 
say, an intensely political experience. Many of the retiring Members are 
veterans who had mastered the art of debate and even while making digs at 
political opponents, have consistently maintained  dignity and decency. I 
believe that decorous debate is the finest form of communication as it 
removes misunderstanding and ensures common good transcending political 
and ideological barriers. 
I am sure, the retiring Members w ill cherish their association with 
this House and the camaraderie with wh ich we all worked together in the 
House. 
I place on record my heartfelt appreciation of the valuable 
contributions the retiring Members have made to the deliberations of the 
House, and the service they have re ndered to Parliamentary democracy. 
Personally, I am grateful for the. consideration they have always shown to me 
in conducting the business of the House. I wish them good health, happiness, 
success and long years of service to  the nation. The House shall ever 
remember their association. 
DR. (SHRIMATI) NAJMA HEPTULLA (Maharashtra): Sir, always 
the procedure is that the Leaders speak and the Members respond. Sir, as you

informs us, at the moment, as to when we are going to have the elections 
because it is only then we will know when we are going to have the next

permanent House. I can understand the feeling of the Lok Sabha Members for

Members who are retiring or rather mo st of them, I know them personally. 
Some of them have been here for two terms, three terms; some have come

stood over here in this seat and bade them farewell with a very heavy heart. I 
know, when one sits on the Chair, it is a tiring job. It is not a very coveted job

part in the discussion. I listened to everything. It has been a very enriching

peaceful

MR. CHAIRMAN: Hon. Members, the second part of the 200 th 
Session, which commenced on Friday, the 30th January, now comes to an end. 
It had four sittings spread over more than 22 hours. During the four days of 
the sittings, important business relating to the Interim Budget (Railways) and 
Interim Budget (General) along with their relevant Appropriation Bills has 
been transacted. Also, the matter regard ing need to declare the States of 
Jharkhand, Chhattisgarh and Uttaranchal as special category States with a 
view to facilitating their comprehensive development as model States, was 
discussed at length through a Private Member's Resolution. 
Besides, the House took up further discussion on the "unemployment 
problem in the country" through a Short Duration Discussion raised in the 
earlier part of the Session. Of course, various matters of Public Importance 
were raised by several Members through Special Mentions. I am happy that 
business all through was conducted in an atmosphere of warm cordiality, 
harmony and understanding. 
I would like to take this opportunity to thank the Leader of the 
House, the Leader of the Opposition, Leaders of various Parties and Groups, 
and all the hon. Members for the kind cooperation extended by them in 
conducting the proceedings of the House. 
I also thank the hon. Deputy Chairman and Members on the panel of 
Vice-Chairmen for their cooperation, as also the Secretariat staff for their hard 
work. 
I, once again, extend my good wishes to the retiring Members.
